description: Somos estudiantes del Gimnasio Campestre con un profundo interés por la programación, la tecnología y la exploración espacial. Formamos parte del equipo de robótica y del programa de Jóvenes Investigadores de nuestro colegio. Además, participamos en el KSC International Space Academy (KSCIA), un programa educativo de la NASA en el que fortalecimos nuestros conocimientos sobre ciencia, ingeniería y exploración espacial. En última instancia queremos usar la ciencia y la programación para aprender.
summary: Living on Red is an interactive web platform with space habitat and colony recreation developed by the Daedalus Team (Bogotá, Colombia) with the use of Python simulation engines. Our platform challenges players to keep human life through hostile environments outside of the planet such as Mar, the Lunar South Pole, Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Deep Space. Nevertheless, instead of treating space survival as a direct process of collecting resources, Living on Red models real environmental control physics combined with life support dynamics. Every simulated Sol (a Martian day) considers the evolution of the user according to its decisions, taking into account the relationship between habitat volume, electrical power, leaks, human intake, and more. By combining a permanent specialist crew roles, progressive unlocks that help the user through their decisions, daily operational choices, and dynamic unpredictable hazards, Living on Red aims to transform aerospace life-support engineering into an accessible training experience for those interested on understanding humans outside of this world.
details:
Overall, Living on Red is an off-world habitat management and life-support simulator. Before launching their mission, users configure their destination environment, choosing between Mars' Jezero Crater, the Lunar South Pole, Low Earth Orbit (LEO), or a Deep Space environment alongside their crew size, target mission duration, and science goal.

Each Sol, being approximately 24 hours in the simulation, involves a five-stage physics and logistical cycle. First, during this period of time, solar power plants generate electricity (a value that changes depending on the location) and supply multiple facility types, including MOXIE oxygen generators, ice extractors, hydroponic crops, and research labs. Next, logistics hubs operated by pilots turn the locally stored production into global colony inventories. At the same time, every cubic meter of an active habitat draws thermal and life-support electricity while losing oxygen and nitrogen to leakage or structural failures. This is, certainly, scaled to each destination's hostility. Meanwhile, each active astronaut consumes about 2000 kcal of food, 2.5 L of water, and approximately 1 kg of oxygen per Sol while exhaling 1 kg of CO2. Finally, a risk algorithm consistently calculates the daily probability of failure from destination hazard rates, average building safety ratings, crew health, and pressurized volume.

Now, to keep the mission operations clear and organized, users are able to control the output of their missions through actions on an organized interface built around crew member roles and progressive unlocks and progress. Each colonist character has a specialty such as Doctor, Engineer, Pilot, etc. and users can open the buildings menu at any time to view workers and enable specialists to work on certain facilities. For daily decisions, an even further simpler action menu allows for five standard set actions alongside five daily directives that activate immediately when they are chosen, while systems such as mining, research synthesis and orbital launches occur gradually as the colony endures longer. When emergencies such as grid overloads or communication breakouts occur, players must coordinate their specialists before life support fails, increasing the difficulty of the game and mirroring reality more closely.

While developing Living on Red, our team made an effort to maintain realistic trade-offs and keep general dynamics that show the snowballing or conflict created because of variable interaction. We built all of our simulation engine, mission control interface, and terminal mode in Python using only standard libraries so anyone can test it, creating accessibility to enable learning. Ultimately, this project is designed as an educational tool and mission-planning sandbox that shows why life-support, resource recycling and the specialization of the crew are needed to sustain life beyond Earth.
